title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
0.1 Aims
This book applies DeCovarT to the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource. It records what is run: the data, the algorithms as implemented, the hyperparameters and their values, the code, the outputs, and which outputs are stale. The reasons behind each choice are in the DeCovarT vignettes; each chapter links to the vignette section that states them and does not restate the theory.
The target is a covariance plug-in for the likelihood, not a biologically interpretable gene regulatory network (03-2, target). Indices follow the article: gene g=1,\ldots,G, type j=1,\ldots,J, bulk sample i=1,\ldots,N, cell c, with C_j cells of type j.

title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
Estimate, for each labelled cell type j at each bulk-matched time, the mean \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and the within-type covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} of a gene panel, on the linear scale that DeCovarT’s convolution needs. The source is one single-specimen scRNA-seq reference (GSE229513, Section 2.1).
Choose that panel for the purpose: genes whose moments can be estimated in every type and that carry information about the proportions \boldsymbol{p} (Section 3.1).
Plug the moments into DeCovarT and deconvolve the bulk series (GSE229386) where a single-cell reference matches it: the standard-Wnt samples at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h.

title: 2  Suppinger gastruloids
text:
2.1 Hierarchical design
Single-cell UMI counts and bulk HTSeq tables come from the murine gastruloid resource of Suppinger and colleagues (Cell Stem Cell, 2023; GEO GSE229513 and GSE229386; (Suppinger et al. 2023)).
The scRNA-seq experiment is one 10x Chromium 3′ v3 resource from one specimen series, not a panel of independent biological replicates. DeCovarT treats it as the one-replicate regime (2.1, one single-cell replicate). Zeros are taken as molecule-sampling counts (Note 4.1). GSE250136 is a later stem-embryo dataset and is not part of this resource.
?fig-suppinger-design draws the two designs side by side.
Single-cell (GSE229513). The first factor is the mESC cell line (B-S or SBR), the second the time slot. Each line covers six slots, and only 48 h is profiled in both. At the three times of the bulk series the cell counts are (output/naive_marker_selection/tables/batch_by_time.csv):
Cell line is therefore confounded with time except at 48 h, and it is not a covariate in any fit of this book. The two lines are treated as one developmental trajectory (Figure 2.3). Gene ranking and covariance estimation run independently at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, the slots with a bulk time point (Section 3.4, Section 4.1). At 48 h the two lines are pooled; Section 3.8 measures what pooling changes.
Bulk RNA-seq (GSE229386). The first factor is the Wnt schedule: the standard pulse at 48 h, or an early pulse at 24 h. The second factor is the time point, 48 h, 72 h or 96 h, each with three biological replicates. No single-cell slot carries the early schedule, so the early-Wnt bulk has no single-cell counterpart at any time. The three single-cell slots used in this book instead match the three time points of the standard-Wnt bulk: single-cell 48 h (B-S and SBR pooled), 72 h (SBR) and 96 h (B-S), each against three biological replicates of the standard-Wnt bulk at that time. The cross-platform filter of Section 3.7 is therefore fitted at all three standard-Wnt time points, never on the early-Wnt arm.

2.2 Seurat processing
Embeddings, QC and clustering follow the Seurat workflow of the Suppinger resource (Suppinger et al. 2023), drawn in Figure 2.1: Alevin counts, scater QC, SCTransform Pearson residuals per batch for integration, CCA, PCA, UMAP and Louvain clustering. Two products of that workflow are used here: the cell-type labels (celltypeannotation), and the gene list of the authors’ SCT counts layer, which serves as the gene allow-list (Section 3.2). The authors’ residuals themselves are not used: the ranking refits SCTransform v2 per time slot (Section 3.4), and the covariances are estimated from raw counts (Section 4.1.2).






Figure 2.1: Seurat workflow used to extract embeddings and downstream analyses on GSE229513.

2.3 Biological interpretation from single-cell compositions
Figure 2.2 and Figure 2.3 summarise a putative reading of annotated type proportions along gastruloid time. They are not a reconstruction of embryonic lineages. Two annotated states are treated as technical artefacts of culture stress (Cd63+ ectoderm-like artefact and Zscan4+ artefact, data/dictionaries/suppinger_celltype_crosswalk.csv). The working caudal sequence after the Chir/Wnt pulse is pluripotency \to epiblast \to primitive streak \to caudal mesoderm / NMP \to pre-somitic mesoderm / somites, with a residual endoderm bias typical of gastruloids.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.1 Scope and status
This chapter builds the gene panel on which the covariances of Section 4.1 are estimated. It is the application that the feature-selection vignette (3.1) leaves to this book: filters as applied, settings, rank tables and code. It runs on the single-cell counts of GSE229513 at the three bulk-matched times (Section 2.1), one time at a time. What the panel must achieve, and why each step is there, is stated in the vignette (3.1, what the genes are for): genes whose type-level moments can be estimated in every type and that carry information about \boldsymbol{p}.
The Suppinger reference is the one-specimen case of that callout. It is one technical scRNA-seq experiment (Suppinger et al. 2023), and its cells are draws from one specimen, not biological replicates (Section 2.1). Every ranking statistic below is therefore computed inside that specimen: it calibrates a screen, not a population-level claim of differential expression. Steps that need several donors, such as a DESeq2 pseudo-bulk shortlist, do not apply here (Section 3.11).
Ranks are computed on SCTransform Pearson residuals or on a count GLM. Neither scale is exported: the moments that enter DeCovarT are on the linear scale (2.1, normalisation).
The current panel (top 500 per time, 1) comes from the between/within ratio. Once the presence gate, the omnibus rank and the bulk filter have been run, they replace that rank as steps 3 to 5 of ?fig-pipeline, and every output of Section 4.1 has to be refitted.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
Note 3.1: ℹ️ Cells are not biological replicates



Treating the cells of one specimen as independent replicates of a population contrast is pseudoreplication: it inflates the apparent sample size and understates the standard error of every statistic computed across cells (Zimmerman et al. 2021; Squair et al. 2021; Crowell et al. 2020). A score fitted this way, or a bootstrap that resamples cells with labels fixed, measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not to new specimens. It is reported as such wherever it is used in this book (Section 4.1, Section 7.2).

text:
3.2 Cell and gene QC as applied
The tiers of quality control recommended in the vignette (3.1, QC) are applied only in part. What runs today is listed here.
Cells.

The authors’ Seurat QC (scater, Section 2.2) is taken as given.
01_01 keeps cells with a time slot in {48 h, 72 h, 96 h}, a non-missing celltypeannotation, and a library size above zero.
The culture-stress labels flagged include_in_ranking = FALSE in data/dictionaries/suppinger_celltype_crosswalk.csv (Cd63+ ectoderm-like artefact, Zscan4+ artefact) are dropped before the fit.
A type with fewer than min_cells = 20 cells in a slot stays in the SCTransform fit and is left out of the scores. Exiting naïve pluripotency at 72 h (8 cells) is the only such case.
No library-size MAD filter, detected-gene filter or mitochondrial filter is applied by this repository. This is the gap with tier (i) of the vignette.

Genes.

The allow-list is the gene set of the authors’ SCT counts layer: 2,944 of the 27,027 genes of the RNA assay. Genes outside it never enter a fit.
After the per-time fit, SCTransform returns residuals for 2,892 (48 h), 2,769 (72 h) and 2,811 (96 h) genes (model_card.csv).
Ribosomal, mitochondrial and sex-chromosome genes are not removed explicitly; whether the authors’ allow-list already excludes them has not been checked.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.3 Presence gate
A gene enters the ranking at a given time only if it is detected, and varies, in every scored type at that time. With \delta_{gj} the fraction of cells of type j with a non-zero count for gene g, and v_{gj} the within-type variance of the counts,

\min_{j}\delta_{gj}\ge\delta_{\min}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\min_{j}v_{gj}>0 .
\tag{3.1}
presence_gate() in R/rank_genes_omnibus.R returns one row per gene with min_detection and a logical pass; \delta_{\min} is the argument min_frac, fixed before the ranks are seen (the sketch below uses 0.05). The reasons for a gate in every type, rather than in at least one, are in 3.1, presence. In the current outputs the gate is absent. Its absence is one cause of the constant-gene fallback described in ?sec-cov-stale.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.4 SCTransform v2 fit per time
rank_genes_sctransform() refits Seurat::SCTransform() separately at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (split_by = "time_point") on the allow-list genes. Cells of every non-artefact type at that time are fitted together. The fitted mean is an intercept plus a library-size offset,

\log\mu_{gc}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\log s_{c},
\qquad
x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{gc},\psi_{g}),
\tag{3.2}
with s_{c} the full RNA library size of cell c (column sum of the unfiltered count matrix, stored as log_umi =\log_{10}s_{c}), not the sum over the allow-list. The Pearson residual is r_{gc}=(x_{gc}-\hat\mu_{gc})/\sqrt{\hat\mu_{gc}+\hat\mu_{gc}^{2}/\hat\psi_{g}}.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.5 Current rank: between/within ratio
The residual matrix of one slot is split by type. With C_j cells of type j, \bar r_{gj} the mean residual of gene g in type j, and v_{gj} its within-type variance, the two decompositions are

\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_{j}\bigl(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{c\in j}\bigl(r_{gc}-\bar r_{gj}\bigr)^{2}
\tag{3.3}
(every cell has weight one), and

\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\bar r_{gj},
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}})^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}v_{gj}
\tag{3.4}
(every type has weight 1/J). The score is the ratio of the between term to the within term. What this ratio estimates, and how it relates to a score test of the type effect, is in 3.1, consistency.
Three lists are built per slot (anova_ss(), anova_ms_equal_type(), rank_ratio()):

Global, equal cell weight. Top n_genes_global = 500 genes by \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}} (ranks_global.csv). The largest type dominates.
Global, equal type weight. Top 500 by \mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within}} (ranks_global_equal_type.csv). This list feeds the export of



Per cell type. One-versus-rest split, top n_genes_celltype = 50 genes by the equal-cell ratio (ranks_per_cell_type.csv). The flag \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}>\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}} is stored and not used as a gate: on unit-variance residuals it is an R^{2}>1/2 cut, which almost no gene meets when one type dominates the slot.

Each list is then united with the signalling markers of the types scored in that slot (Section 3.9).

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.6 Omnibus count-model rank
rank_genes_omnibus() (R/rank_genes_omnibus.R) replaces the residual ratio by a test of the cell-type main effect on the counts, then ranks the genes that pass by effect size. Per time slot, on the genes that pass the presence gate:

Fit the negative-binomial GLM \log\mu_{gc}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{g,j(c)}+\log s_{c} with glmGamPoi::glm_gp(design = ~ cell_type, offset = log(s_c)) (Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber 2020). The offset is the full library size; size_factors is switched off so that it is not applied twice.
Test the joint type effect with glmGamPoi::test_de(fit, reduced_design = ~ 1): the quasi-likelihood F test of Lund et al. (2012) as implemented in glmGamPoi. The gate is a Benjamini–Hochberg threshold on adj_pval.
Rank the genes that pass by an effect size, the deviance explained R^{2}_{D,g}=1-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)/\mathcal{D}_g(M_0), with the types weighted equally as in Equation 3.4.


# Not run. counts: genes x cells of one slot; cell_type: factor over
# cells; lib: full library sizes (10^log_umi). Thresholds are set
# before the ranks are seen.
source("R/rank_genes_omnibus.R")
gate <- presence_gate(counts, cell_type, min_frac = 0.05)
keep <- gate$gene[gate$pass]
size_factors <- lib / stats::median(lib)
# rank_genes_omnibus() applies the same gate internally (min_frac).
ranked <- rank_genes_omnibus(
  counts,
  cell_type,
  size_factors = size_factors,
  fdr = 0.05,
  min_frac = 0.05,
  n_select = 500L
)
panel <- ranked$gene[ranked$selected]

# The two glmGamPoi calls it wraps (size factors through the offset):
fit <- glmGamPoi::glm_gp(
  counts[keep, ],
  design = ~cell_type,
  col_data = data.frame(cell_type = cell_type),
  offset = log(size_factors),
  size_factors = rep(1, ncol(counts))
)
qlf <- glmGamPoi::test_de(fit, reduced_design = ~1)

The wrapper arguments in the chunk are illustrative; the definitive signatures are those of R/rank_genes_omnibus.R. Why a gate followed by an effect size, rather than a rank by p-value, is in 3.1, omnibus.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.7 Bulk consistency filter
bulk_consistency_filter() (R/bulk_consistency.R) removes genes whose bulk expression cannot be produced by the single-cell reference. It needs a single-cell slot and a bulk sample of the same condition (?fig-suppinger-design).

Matched pairs. The single-cell reference matches the standard-Wnt bulk at all three times used in this book: single-cell 48 h (B-S and SBR pooled), 72 h (SBR) and 96 h (B-S), each against three biological replicates of the standard-Wnt bulk at that time.
No match for early Wnt. The early-Wnt bulk (Wnt pulse at 24 h) has no single-cell counterpart at any time, so no bulk–reference comparison is possible on that arm.
Fit. At each of the three matched times independently: for each gene, compare the bulk value of each replicate with the range that the type means of that time allow, and flag median-absolute-deviation outliers. The range is the bound of 3.1, cross-platform consistency, and the thresholds follow RNA-Sieve’s range bound and outlier rule (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021).
Apply. A gene flagged at any of the three matched times is removed from the panel at every time, including the early-Wnt arm, where no matched pair exists.
Assumption, now testable. With three matched times the flags can be compared across 48 h, 72 h and 96 h: a gene flagged consistently supports treating the platform effect as a property of the gene, a gene flagged only at one time does not. This comparison has not yet been run.
Status. A heuristic, labelled as such in the code. No script reads the bulk HTSeq table yet (01_01 does not); the filter has not been run.

In the vignette, cross-platform consistency is a perspective, not a tier: its review table gives DeCovarT no cross-platform step, because the reference is one specimen (3.1, comparison of second-generation methods). For Suppinger, the entry of that column is the range bound fitted at 48 h described here. The model behind the bound, its tail (3.1, tail bound), and the alternatives that keep such genes and down-weight them are in the vignette.

# Not run. sc[[tm]]: raw counts (genes x cells) of the single-cell slot
# at time tm, with labels cell_type[[tm]] and full library sizes
# lib[[tm]]; bulk[[tm]]: the three standard-Wnt replicates at tm from
# GSE229386 (genes x samples), same gene identifiers.
source("R/utils_general.R")
source("R/bulk_consistency.R")
flags <- lapply(c("48h", "72h", "96h"), function(tm) {
  x <- sc[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE]
  ct <- droplevels(factor(cell_type[[tm]]))
  norm <- sweep(as.matrix(x), 2L, lib[[tm]] / stats::median(lib[[tm]]), "/")
  mu <- sapply(levels(ct), function(k) rowMeans(norm[, ct == k, drop = FALSE]))
  sd <- sapply(levels(ct), function(k) apply(norm[, ct == k, drop = FALSE], 1L, stats::sd))
  out <- bulk_consistency_filter(
    bulk = bulk[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE],
    mu = mu,
    sd = sd,
    n_cells = table(ct)[levels(ct)],
    z_range = 3,
    mad_k = 3
  )
  out$gene[!out$keep]
})
panel <- setdiff(panel, unique(unlist(flags)))

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.8 Cell-line sensitivity at 48 h
48 h is the only slot that contains both cell lines. The script output/naive_marker_selection/cell_line_48h/01_03_sensitivity_48h_cell_line.R refits the same v2 model inside B-S and inside SBR and compares the equal-cell top 500 and the per-type top 50. (It lives under output/ next to its results; scripts/01_03_export_equal_type_seurat.R is a different script.)

The two global lists share 308 of 500 genes (Jaccard 0.45).
Epiblast shares 29, and exiting naïve pluripotency 30, of its top 50.
Naïve pluripotency is scored in SBR only: B-S has fewer than 20 cells of that type.

Outputs: overlap_48h_cell_line.csv, ranks_global_48h_by_line.csv, ranks_per_cell_type_48h_by_line.csv, venn_48h_cell_line.pdf.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.9 Knowledge-driven markers
The marker list is curated and short: data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv, with columns cell_type_excel (lineage on the signalling map), cell_type_suppinger (the matching Suppinger label, or NA) and gene_marker. Symbols are mapped offline with org.Mm.eg.db (R/map_marker_symbols.R), not biomaRt.
Fifteen of the 19 mouse symbols are in the 2,944-gene allow-list. Under a uniform draw of 19 genes from the 27,027 RNA symbols the expected overlap is about 2.1; the hypergeometric upper tail is P(X\ge 15)=8.8\times10^{-12} (marker_sct_hypergeometric.csv). The four absent markers are Myod1, Pax6, Sox1 and Tfap2a (venn_markers_vs_counts.pdf).

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.11 Optional multivariate refinement
A univariate rank ignores redundancy between genes and the covariances DeCovarT models. The optional stage searches subsets of the panel with a multi-objective criterion on all types jointly (3.1, covariance-driven (post hoc) selection). It needs \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}, so it runs after Section 4.1, and it is drawn dashed in ?fig-pipeline. Its panels fall under the circularity warning of the vignette (3.1, circularity): a comparison with other methods also reports the panel of 1, chosen without the model.
Shortlist. The multi-donor pipeline of the screening appendix (S6, multi-donor pipeline) feeds NSGA-II with a DESeq2 pseudo-bulk shortlist. With one specimen, as for the Suppinger reference, the DESeq2 step does not apply, and strategy B of that appendix (presence gate, omnibus gate, effect-size rank; Section 3.3 and Section 3.6) replaces the shortlist.
Types with few cells. A joint test or objective on the panel \mathcal{G} uses the within-type covariance, which is high-dimensional when C_j is not much larger than |\mathcal{G}| (3.1, multivariate tests). With the 500-gene panel of 1, seven of the eleven scored type × time cells of Table 3.2 have C_j<|\mathcal{G}|, so their sample covariance is singular:

48 h: exiting naïve pluripotency (265 cells), naïve pluripotency (36);
72 h: ectopic pluripotency (266), naïve pluripotency (66);
96 h: gut (140), ectopic pluripotency (116), somite differentiation front (29).

Caudal mesoderm at 96 h (1,061 cells) is about twice the panel size. For these types the objectives below use the regularised \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of Section 4.1, never the sample covariance.
Planned settings:

Optimiser. NSGA-II through mco::nsga2() (Mersmann et al. 2020). Genes are encoded as a mask in [0,1]^{G}, thresholded to a target panel size.
Objectives, all minimised:

the 2-norm condition number \kappa_{2}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathcal{G}}) of the mean signature restricted to the panel;
the mean pairwise MixSim overlap of the J Gaussians \mathcal{N}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}) (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021);
optionally, minus the smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information for \boldsymbol{p}, as a sensitivity objective on a shortlist of non-dominated panels.

Output. The whole Pareto front, not one panel. With one specimen, any panel chosen here is fitted on this atlas and has to be challenged on an external gastruloid cohort.

title: 4  Covariance estimation

4.1 Scope and status
This chapter estimates, for each scored cell type j at each bulk-matched time, the mean \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and the within-type covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of the gene panel of Section 3.10, and exports them on the linear scale of DeCovarT’s convolution,
\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\succ 0 .
\tag{4.1}
The target is the covariance that enters the likelihood, not a mechanistic gene network; a dense estimate is therefore an acceptable plug-in and is the default (3.2, target).
Nothing in this chapter has produced a usable covariance yet. The outputs that exist are stale and are kept only as a record of what went wrong (?sec-cov-stale).

4.2.1 Shrinkage covariance (default)
fit_cov_shrinkage() calls corpcor::cov.shrink() (Schäfer et al. 2021) with the Schäfer–Strimmer target D: variances kept, correlations shrunk towards zero by a common factor (Schäfer and Strimmer 2005). corpcor 1.6.10 also shrinks the variances towards their median by default; lambda.var = 0 switches that off, so the target is exactly D. The closed-form intensity \hat\lambda^{\ast} (corpcor::estimate.lambda()) is the centre of the grid, and cross-validation picks the value used. The estimate is positive definite for any C_j and G, so it is the estimator used when the others fail. The theory is in 3.2, shrinkage. corpcor is not in renv.lock.


4.2.2 Graphical lasso with an unpenalised diagonal
fit_cov_glasso() standardises the panel, fits glasso::glasso(R, rho = lambda, penalize.diagonal = FALSE) (Friedman et al. 2019) on the sample correlation \boldsymbol{R}_j by block coordinate descent (Friedman et al. 2008), and rescales: \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\Delta_j^{-1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}\Delta_j^{-1/2} with \Delta_j=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{V}_j) (rescale_correlation_fit()). With the diagonal unpenalised the fitted correlation keeps a unit diagonal, so \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} matches the sample variances.

penalize.diagonal defaults to TRUE in glasso 1.11; it is set explicitly.
huge (Zhao et al. 2022) is not used: huge.glasso() always penalises the diagonal and has no switch for it (checked in the huge 1.5.1 sources). The reasons are in 3.3, graphical lasso.
Grid endpoints come from lambda_endpoints(): at \lambda_{\max}=\max_{g\neq g'}|R_{gg'}| the off-diagonal precision is zero; the lower end is of order \sqrt{\log G/C_j}.
A gene constant across the cells of a type is left out of that type’s fit and listed in excluded_genes, instead of forcing a diagonal covariance for all genes.
A penalty whose solve fails is dropped from the grid and listed in failed_lambda, instead of being replaced by a diagonal precision.

The earlier selector, a safeguarded EBIC interval search (ebic_adaptive_path(), at most n_solves = 40 solves, \gamma=0.5 (Foygel and Drton 2010)), is kept in scripts/03_01_grn_huge.R as a diagnostic path. It no longer chooses \lambda.

The object kept is the support at level \alpha (global_decision), not the dense de-sparsified matrix.

An SPD refit on the linear-scale panel under the zeros of that support, with glasso::glasso(V, rho = 0, zero = ..., penalize.diagonal = FALSE).

The script scripts/03_02_grn_silggm.R (seed 1, \alpha=0.05) stops after step 2 and has never been run; the refit lives in the wrapper.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{PLNnetwork: alternating graphical lasso and variational updates} \begin{algorithmic} \Require counts $X$, offsets $O=\log s$, penalty $\lambda$, weights $W$ \State initialise the variational means $M$, variances $S$ and $\Sigma$ \For{$h = 1,\ldots,$ maxit\_out} \State $\Omega^{(h)} \gets$ \Call{GraphicalLasso}{$\Sigma^{(h-1)}, \lambda W$} \State $(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)}) \gets$ \Call{NLopt}{$B^{(h-1)},M^{(h-1)},S^{(h-1)};\Omega^{(h)}$} \State $\Sigma^{(h)} \gets C^{-1}\left[{M^{(h)}}^\top M^{(h)} + \sum_c S_c^{(h)}\right]$ \State $F_h \gets -\mathrm{ELBO}(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)},\Omega^{(h)}) + \lambda\|\Omega^{(h)}\|_{1,W}$ \If{$|F_h-F_{h-1}|/|F_h| <$ ftol\_out} \State \textbf{break} \EndIf \EndFor \State \Return $(B,M,S,\Omega,\Sigma)$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Algorithm 4.1 is the block-coordinate scheme of Chiquet et al. (2018). The model, the variational bound and the role of the offset are in 3.3, PLN.
The latent moments (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}) are not on DeCovarT’s scale. pln_linear_moments() maps them to the moments of the counts, averaged over the size factors s_c of the cells being scored:

\mathbb{E}\,x_{gc}=s_{c}\,e^{\mu_{z,g}+\sigma_{z,gg}/2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c})
+
\bigl(\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\,\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}^{\top}\bigr)
\circ
\bigl(e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigr),
\tag{4.3}
with e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}} taken entrywise. The moments are then divided by the size factor, so that the four estimators are scored on the same size-factor-normalised table.

title: 4  Covariance estimation
text:
4.3 Cross-validation and outputs
The same loss selects the tuning parameter of every estimator and compares the four: the held-out Gaussian log-likelihood on the linear scale. For held-out cells \mathcal{T} and an estimate (\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) fitted without them,

\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}};\mathcal{T})
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{T}}
\log\phi_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c};\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\bigr),
\tag{4.4}
computed by heldout_gaussian_logscore() through a Cholesky factor of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}. Why this score is a legitimate loss for the covariance even though cells are not Gaussian, and why it replaces AIC, BIC and EBIC as the selector, is in 3.2, cross-validation.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Tuning by K-fold cross-validation, and nested comparison of the four estimators} \begin{algorithmic} \Procedure{CVSelect}{$X, f, \Lambda, K$} \State split the cells of $X$ into $K$ folds at random, with a fixed seed \For{$\lambda \in \Lambda$} \For{$k = 1,\ldots,K$} \State $(\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma) \gets f(X_{-k};\lambda)$ \State $\ell_k(\lambda) \gets$ \Call{HeldOutLogScore}{$\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma,X_k$} \EndFor \State $m(\lambda) \gets$ mean of $\ell_k(\lambda)$; $\mathrm{se}(\lambda) \gets$ its standard error \EndFor \State $\lambda_{\min} \gets \arg\max_{\lambda} m(\lambda)$ \State $\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}} \gets$ most regularised $\lambda$ with $m(\lambda) \ge m(\lambda_{\min}) - \mathrm{se}(\lambda_{\min})$ \State \Return $(m, \mathrm{se}, \lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{1\mathrm{se}})$ \EndProcedure \Procedure{NestedCompare}{$X, \{(f_e,\Lambda_e)\}_{e=1}^{4}, K_{\mathrm{out}}, K_{\mathrm{in}}$} \For{$k = 1,\ldots,K_{\mathrm{out}}$} \For{$e = 1,\ldots,4$} \State $\lambda_e \gets \lambda_{\min}$ of \Call{CVSelect}{$X_{-k}, f_e, \Lambda_e, K_{\mathrm{in}}$} \State $(\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma) \gets f_e(X_{-k};\lambda_e)$ \State $s_{ek} \gets$ \Call{HeldOutLogScore}{$\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma,X_k$} \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $(s_{ek})$, paired by outer fold \EndProcedure \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Settings in scripts/03_04_cv_covariance.R:

cv_select_tuning(X, fit_fun, grid, K = 5, seed) returns the mean and standard error per grid value and the min and 1se choices. The exported fit uses min; 1se is reported beside it.
nested_cv_compare(X, estimators, K_outer = 5, K_inner = 5, seed) is run only to compare the four estimators. The inner loop chooses the tuning parameter, the outer loop scores the chosen fit on cells it never saw.
Folds split cells of one unit. The score measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not to new specimens (Note 3.1).
In units with very few cells (29 cells for the somite differentiation front) each training fold has about 23 cells; the shrinkage estimate is the only one expected to be stable there.

Diagnostics that are computed but do not select: the EBIC path of the graphical lasso (Section 4.2.2), and edge stability under subsampling. StARS is not run: with 20 subsamples and 40 penalties it costs about 800 graphical-lasso solves per unit, against 40 for the EBIC path.

For the estimator retained for a unit, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} is the mean of the size-factor-normalised counts of its cells and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} is the selected covariance, both on the scale of Section 4.1.2; Equation 4.1 holds by construction. For PLNnetwork both come from Equation 4.3. Which covariance layer these cell-level moments identify, and how the sample scales are estimated inside the DeCovarT fit, is in 2.1, three regimes and 2.1, profile Newton.


4.3.1 Displays
Plot functions are in R/plot_grn_regularisation.R. Each display answers one question.
Choosing the tuning parameter (one unit, one estimator).

Cross-validation curve: m(\lambda)\pm\mathrm{se}(\lambda) against the tuning parameter, with the min and 1se choices marked (new; not produced yet).
Regularisation path: each off-diagonal entry of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda) against \log\lambda, five edges that survive at the selected \lambda and five that are driven to zero (graphical lasso, PLNnetwork).
EBIC against \log\lambda, and EBIC against edge density |E|/\{G(G-1)/2\} (diagnostic only).

Comparing estimators (one unit).

Outer-fold held-out scores s_{ek} of Algorithm 4.2, one line per fold across the four estimators, so that the comparison is paired.
Partial-correlation heatmaps at the selected tuning parameter, with one gene order frozen across estimators and types, 
\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}
=
-\frac{\omega_{gg'}}{\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}}},
\tag{4.5} on a diverging scale centred at zero.
For the three sparse estimators: UpSet plots of edge presence and of signed edges.

Comparing types (one time). Pairwise Hellinger distance and MixSim overlap between the exported Gaussians on the linear scale (gaussian_hellinger(), gaussian_mixsim_overlap() in R/ebic_regularisation_path.R). Distances computed on another scale (nonparanormal scores, \log(1+x)) do not describe what DeCovarT has to separate.


4.3.2 Evaluation
There is no ground-truth network for murine gastruloids, and the estimand is a covariance. The scores are therefore relative, in this order of weight:

Held-out likelihood, outer folds of Algorithm 4.2: the selector, and the only score that compares all four estimators on one scale.
Downstream deconvolution: DeCovarT error on the matched 48 h bulk and in the misspecification sweep of Section 7.1, with \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} from each estimator. This is the score tied to the paper’s estimand.
Technical stability: a bootstrap of cells within type, labels fixed (Note 3.1). Edge-inclusion frequencies for the sparse estimators and the Frobenius spread of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} for all four. Conditional on this specimen.
Separation of types: Hellinger and MixSim overlap of



Concordance of the sparse estimators: overlap of edge sets (intersection over the smaller set) and Hamming distance between skeletons, raw and divided by G(G-1)/2. Agreement is a robustness number, not a validation.

Scores that need a known skeleton, curated transcription-factor targets, other assays or perturbations are perspectives (3.3, perspectives).






Note 4.1: ℹ️ No zero-inflation layer



Suppinger is droplet UMI data. Zeros are modelled as Poisson or negative-binomial sampling zeros (Svensson 2020); no estimator in this book has a zero-inflation or hurdle layer. Zero-inflated observation models appear only as a contamination in Section 7.1.

title: 5  Applying and comparing deconvolution outputs applied to Suppinger study
text:
5.1 What is being compared
DeCovarT deconvolves bulk profiles with both a mean signature and a per-type covariance. Every method below uses the same gene panel and the same labelled single-cell reference; they differ in what they model beyond the mean. All runs are planned on GSE229386, at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, for the standard Wnt pulse and the early pulse (Section 2.1). Each model is reviewed in 5.1, review; one line here says what it models and how it is called.

title: 5  Applying and comparing deconvolution outputs applied to Suppinger study
text:
5.1.1 Second-generation, mean-based

BayesPrism (Chu et al. 2022) — a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with the single-cell reference as a prior on cell-type expression, updated by Gibbs sampling. R, BayesPrism: new.prism(), run.prism(), get.fraction().
SCDC (Dong et al. 2021) — weighted non-negative least squares with clipped gene weights, and an ensemble over several references. With one reference the ensemble step does nothing. R, SCDC: SCDC_prop(), or SCDC_prop_ONE() for a one-subject reference.
DWLS (Tsoucas et al. 2019) — dampened weighted least squares, weights the inverse squared fitted mean, capped by a dampening constant. R, DWLS: solveDampenedWLS().




5.1.2 Single-cell likelihood strategy

DeCovarT, profile Newton — the linear single-cell layer, with \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} weighted by p_{ji} and both sample scales profiled out, maximised by trust-region Newton in ILR coordinates (2.1, profile Newton). R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "newton").
DeCovarT, Levenberg–Marquardt — the released population convolution, covariance \sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, maximised by marqLevAlg in ILR coordinates. With a one-specimen reference the quadratic slot is the wrong one (2.1, one replicate); the fit is the reference point for the released model. R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_Marquardt_Levenberg().
RNA-Sieve (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021) — genes independent; a central-limit Gaussian bulk whose variance is linear in the cell count, with the reference means as noisy regressors and sandwich intervals. Python, rnasieve (songlab-cal/rna-sieve): model_from_raw_counts(), then predict().
MEAD (Xie and Wang 2023) — an estimating equation corrected for reference measurement error, with gene–gene dependence in the sandwich variance and intervals for \boldsymbol{p}. R, MEAD (DongyueXie/MEAD): MEAD().
ReDeconv (Lu et al. 2025) — keeps the transcriptome size S_j in the reference, corrects gene length on the bulk side only, and models the within-type variance through a central-limit law over cells. Code jyyulab/redeconv; entry point to be taken from its tutorial.



5.1.3 Gold-standard baselines

NNLS — non-negative least squares on the mean signature, then projection on the simplex; homoscedastic, mean only. R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_nnls(), which calls nnls::nnls().
Robust linear regression (RLM) — Huber M-estimation of \boldsymbol{y}\approx\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, which down-weights outlying genes. R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_rlm(), which calls MASS::rlm(method = "M").

# G x G x J covariances for the population convolution. Same panel and
# reference for every method.
fit_newton <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_single_cell(
  y, mu, sigma_w, optimiser = "newton"
)
fit_ml <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_Marquardt_Levenberg(
  y, mu, sigma_pop
)
fit_nnls <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_nnls(y, mu)
fit_rlm <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_rlm(y, mu)

from rnasieve.preprocessing import model_from_raw_counts
model, cleaned_bulks = model_from_raw_counts(reference_counts, bulks)
proportions = model.predict(cleaned_bulks)

title: 6  Early versus standard Wnt
text:
6.1 Biological insights from deconvolution algorithms applied to mouse gastruloids
Figure 6.1 contrasts a standard Wnt pulse at 48 h with a premature pulse at 24 h, at three bulk-matched time points: 48 h, 72 h and 96 h. Section 6.1.1 says what the figure can and cannot support; 1 gives the biological reading.

title: 6  Early versus standard Wnt
text:
6.1.1 The figure and its statistical reading






Figure 6.1: Deconvolution-guided comparison of standard versus early Wnt gastruloids at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h.





Figure 6.1 is a raster illustration, not a plot of estimates. Panels A and B draw trajectories; the six bar thumbnails of panel C carry no axis, scale or value. No deconvolution output exists in this repository yet: the comparator runs of Section 5.1 are planned, not run. What follows reads the figure qualitatively and lists what its claims would need. Readings marked (ours) are not in the figure.

The consensus is on direction, not on point estimates. Panel C reports that BayesPrism, SCDC and DWLS agree on the direction of change between arms (ectopic pluripotency up, primitive streak and pre-somitic mesoderm down in the early arm) and not on absolute abundances. Only that direction is carried into



Why absolute abundances disagree. The figure attributes the disagreement to weighted least squares and marker weighting, which are sensitive to collinearity among closely related states. When neighbouring states have close mean profiles on the panel (candidates here, not yet checked: naïve, exiting naïve and epiblast at 48 h; pre-somitic mesoderm and somite differentiation front at 96 h), the signature is ill-conditioned, and a small change of gene weights moves mass between neighbours (3.1, condition number). (Ours.) Collinearity affects every method that inverts the same signature, BayesPrism included; it separates methods only through their weights. Panel C groups SCDC, a weighted least squares, with BayesPrism, a multinomial likelihood, and sets DWLS apart, which points at the dampened weights of DWLS (Tsoucas et al. 2019) rather than at least squares as such. Testing this needs the condition number of the panel signature at each time and the per-method estimates.
Why direction can agree when levels do not. (Ours.) At one time both arms are deconvolved with the same reference and panel. A method bias that multiplies the proportion of a type by a fixed factor cancels in the log-ratio contrast between arms; a bias that moves mass between collinear neighbours depends on the sample and does not cancel. Proportions are also closed: a rise of ectopic pluripotency forces other types down, so “ectopic pluripotency up” and “primitive streak down” are not two independent findings. The redraw therefore reads contrasts on centred log-ratios within each sample.
Uncertainty the claims need. (Ours.)

A per-algorithm interval for every proportion: from the method’s own uncertainty model where it has one (BayesPrism samples a posterior), and from resampling reference cells within type otherwise, which also carries the uncertainty of the one-specimen reference (Section 2.1).
A bootstrap over bulk replicates within arm and time, since the replicate is the unit of the arm effect, not the gene or the cell. There are three replicates per arm and time (?fig-suppinger-design), so a resample takes only 10 distinct values per arm; the redraw shows the nine pairwise early-minus-standard differences beside the percentile interval.
Panel C also states that control gastruloids vary more. A variance from three replicates has two degrees of freedom, and its 95 % chi-square interval spans a factor of about 150, so that claim needs more replicates or a model that pools across types and times.

How to read agreement across methods. (Ours.) The methods share the reference, the panel and the bulk, so their errors are correlated, and agreement of three methods is not three independent confirmations. Two failure modes are shared by all of them. The early-Wnt bulk has no single-cell counterpart at any time (Section 3.7), so a state specific to that arm is forced onto the nearest reference types. And several states drawn in panels A and B (caudal epiblast, neuromesodermal progenitors) are not among the scored reference types of Table 3.2, so no deconvolution against those references can return them. Sign agreement across methods is therefore necessary, not sufficient. A proposed reporting rule for the redraw: call a direction when every method gives the same sign and, for each method, the nine replicate pairs share that sign; report a per-sample goodness of fit on the early arm beside it.



6.1.2 Biological interpretation
On the control-like arm, 72 h is primitive-streak enriched and 96 h shows pre-somitic mesoderm and somite progression. On the early Wnt arm, 48 h retains more naïve pluripotency, 72 h is dominated by ectopic pluripotency with a reduced primitive streak, and 96 h nearly loses pre-somitic mesoderm. Absolute abundances disagree across algorithms (Section 6.1.1), so we treat the direction of change (ectopic pluripotency up, primitive streak and pre-somitic mesoderm down) as the consensus, not the point estimates.




Tsoucas, Daphne, Rui Dong, Haide Chen, Qian Zhu, Guoji Guo, and Guo-Cheng Yuan. 2019. “Accurate Estimation of Cell-Type Composition from Gene Expression Data.” Nature Communications 10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-10802-z.

title: 7  Sensitivity analyses
text:
7.2 scDesign3 settings for GSE229513
The fitted count simulator of S5, simulator draws reference-like cells whose type-level law is known. On Suppinger it is used to calibrate, not to resample: the cells of one specimen series are not biological replicates (Note 3.1).



Table 7.1: scDesign3 settings per type and time for GSE229513.









Setting
Value




Fit unit
One model per time slot, 48 h, 72 h and 96 h; the two lines pooled at 48 h, cell line not a covariate (Section 2.1)


Cells and genes
Cells after QC, culture-stress labels removed (Section 3.2); the selected panel, raw UMI counts (Section 4.1.2)


Margins
Negative binomial, mean and dispersion by cell type, log size factor as mean offset; no zero inflation (Note 4.1)


Copula
Gaussian, one per type, correlation of the plug-in \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of that type and time (Section 4.2.1); not refitted


Composition and depth
Type proportions C_j/\sum_\ell C_\ell of the slot, frozen; each synthetic cell takes the size factor of a real cell of its type


Truth for scoring
Count-scale mean and covariance of a large draw (for example 10^{5} cells per type), not \boldsymbol{R}_j


Checks before use
Normal QQ plots of randomised quantile residuals per gene and type; marginal and copula AIC and BIC against independence and the empirical copula






Factors of the list above that the simulator serves:

1, observation noise: negative-binomial cells replace the Gaussian law; pseudo-bulks are sums of simulated cells at known \boldsymbol{p}.
2, missing component: simulate every type and leave one out of the signature.
3, copula dependence: swap the plug-in correlation for an equicorrelated or a Clayton copula, margins fixed.
6, wrong covariance reference: generate with the \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of one estimator or time, and fit DeCovarT with another.

Spillover (4) and outlier genes (5) are added after generation; the simulator plays no part in them.

title: 7  Sensitivity analyses
text:
7.3 Signature size and selection threshold
S5i, signature size states the hypothesis: accuracy rises with the number of genes, reaches a plateau, then falls once uninformative genes or genes inconsistent between bulk and single-cell libraries enter the panel. Every chapter of this book so far uses one panel, the top n_genes_global = 500 of the type-equal ratio (Section 3.5, Section 3.10). This section plans the sweep that tests the hypothesis on GSE229513. It has not been run.



Table 7.2: Factors of the panel-size sweep. The largest panel stays below the size of the allow-list of every slot (Section 3.2).









Factor
Levels




Panel size n_genes_global
50; 100; 200; 500; 1000; 2000, the top genes of each rank


Rank
type-equal ratio (ranks_global_equal_type.csv, column rank); omnibus rank (deviance_r2_equal_type, Section 3.6)


Omnibus gate
Benjamini–Hochberg level fdr of rank_genes_omnibus(): 0.001; 0.01; 0.05; 0.2


Bulk consistency filter
off; on (Section 3.7)


Time slot
48 h, 72 h, 96 h (Section 2.1)


Methods
NNLS; DeCovarT, profile Newton (Section 5.1)






Design choices:

Source of genes. The 500-gene export data/intermediate/equal_type_top500_by_time.rds cannot supply panels larger than 500. The sweep reads the allow-list object data/intermediate/suppinger_sct_allowlist_seurat.rds and the full rank table, then subsets genes per panel size.
Truth. Within each type, cells are split at random into a reference half and a pseudo-bulk half. The rank, the mean and the covariance use the reference half only; pseudo-bulks are sums of cells of the other half at known numbers per type. Bulk and reference cells are then disjoint, the condition under which a within-type variance can matter (S5, ReDeconv). Both halves come from one specimen series, so the pseudo-bulks carry no platform bias and no between-specimen variation (Note 3.1).
Platform-inconsistent genes. The pseudo-bulks cannot reveal them. The real standard-Wnt bulks of GSE229386 enter through the bulk consistency filter: the sweep is repeated on the panels with the flagged genes removed, and on the real bulks the change of \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} with panel size is reported, since no truth exists there.
Scale. Means, covariances and pseudo-bulks use raw UMI counts, so a pseudo-bulk is an exact sum of the cell profiles. The size-factor scale of Section 4.1.2 is a second arm.
Metrics. DeCovarT::compute_benchmark_metrics() with the true cell fractions: total variation and RMSE per bulk (regression$global), and per-type correlation and error (regression$cell_type). For the real bulks, the total variation between \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} at each size and at 500 genes.

The covariance has G(G+1)/2 entries per type. Above the number of reference cells of a type the sample covariance is singular, and only the shrinkage estimate of Section 4.2.1 is defined; the closed-form intensity is used in the sweep rather than cross-validation, to keep the cost linear in the number of panels.

# Not run. Function names and arguments follow R/rank_genes_omnibus.R,
# R/cv_covariance_selection.R and the DeCovarT reference; corpcor and
# nnls are not in renv.lock. Culture-stress labels are removed first,
# as in scripts/01_03_export_equal_type_seurat.R.
source("R/utils_general.R")
source("R/rank_genes_omnibus.R")
source("R/cv_covariance_selection.R")

seu <- readRDS("data/intermediate/suppinger_sct_allowlist_seurat.rds")
ranks <- utils::read.csv(
  "output/naive_marker_selection/tables/ranks_global_equal_type.csv"
)
panel_sizes <- c(50L, 100L, 200L, 500L, 1000L, 2000L)
bh_levels <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.2)
time_level <- "48h"
n_bulk <- 100L
n_cells_bulk <- 500L

counts <- assay_matrix(seu, "RNA", "counts")
in_slot <- seu$time_point == time_level # & !culture-stress label
x <- as.matrix(counts[, in_slot])
cell_type <- droplevels(factor(seu$celltypeannotation[in_slot]))
lib <- 10^seu$log_umi[in_slot]
types <- levels(cell_type)

# Disjoint halves within each type: 1 = reference, 2 = pseudo-bulk.
half <- withr::with_seed(20261101, {
  stats::ave(
    seq_along(cell_type),
    cell_type,
    FUN = function(i) sample(rep_len(1:2, length(i)))
  )
})
ref <- half == 1L

# Rank A: type-equal ratio of the current pipeline (computed on all
# cells of the slot; rank B below is the leakage-free one).
rank_a <- ranks[ranks$time_point == time_level & !is.na(ranks$rank), ]
rank_a <- rank_a$gene[order(rank_a$rank)]

# Rank B: omnibus rank on the reference half; fdr = 1 keeps every gene
# so that each BH level is a filter of one fit.
omni <- rank_genes_omnibus(
  x[, ref],
  cell_type[ref],
  size_factors = lib[ref] / stats::median(lib[ref]),
  fdr = 1,
  n_select = max(panel_sizes)
)
omni <- omni[!is.na(omni$rank), ]
rank_b <- lapply(bh_levels, function(level) {
  gated <- omni[omni$adj_pval <= level, ]
  gated$gene[order(gated$rank)]
})
names(rank_b) <- paste0("omnibus_fdr_", bh_levels)

# Pseudo-bulks at known cell numbers, from the pseudo-bulk half.
pseudo <- withr::with_seed(20261102, {
  lapply(seq_len(n_bulk), function(b) {
    w <- stats::rgamma(length(types), shape = 2)
    m <- stats::rmultinom(1L, n_cells_bulk, prob = w / sum(w))[, 1L]
    cells <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(types), function(j) {
      pool <- which(!ref & cell_type == types[j])
      pool[sample.int(length(pool), m[j], replace = TRUE)]
    }))
    list(y = rowSums(x[, cells, drop = FALSE]), p = m / sum(m))
  })
})

fit_panel <- function(genes) {
  mu <- vapply(
    types,
    function(j) rowMeans(x[genes, ref & cell_type == j, drop = FALSE]),
    numeric(length(genes))
  )
  sigma <- vapply(
    types,
    function(j) {
      xj <- t(x[genes, ref & cell_type == j, drop = FALSE])
      fit_cov_shrinkage(xj, lambda = shrinkage_lambda_closed_form(xj))$sigma
    },
    matrix(0, length(genes), length(genes))
  )
  scores <- lapply(pseudo, function(pb) {
    y <- pb$y[genes]
    p_nnls <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_nnls(y, mu)
    p_dcv <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_single_cell(y, mu, sigma)$p
    rbind(
      cbind(
        method = "nnls",
        DeCovarT::compute_benchmark_metrics(
          y, mu, estimated_p = p_nnls, true_ratios = pb$p
        )$regression$global
      ),
      cbind(
        method = "decovart_newton",
        DeCovarT::compute_benchmark_metrics(
          y, mu, estimated_p = p_dcv, true_ratios = pb$p
        )$regression$global
      )
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, scores)
}

rank_lists <- c(list(type_equal_ratio = rank_a), rank_b)
sweep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(rank_lists), function(r) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(panel_sizes, function(n) {
    genes <- utils::head(rank_lists[[r]], n)
    if (length(genes) < n) {
      return(NULL) # the gate passes fewer genes than requested
    }
    cbind(rank = r, n_genes_global = n, fit_panel(genes))
  }))
}))

# Bulk consistency filter on the real standard-Wnt bulks of the slot
# (bulk: genes x 3 replicates, same identifiers). sd and n_cells come
# from the reference half; flagged genes are removed before the sweep
# is repeated.
# flags <- bulk_consistency_filter(bulk, mu = mu_all, sd = sd_all,
#                                  n_cells = table(cell_type[ref]))
# rank_lists_clean <- lapply(rank_lists, intersect, flags$gene[flags$keep])

Three outcomes would bear on the hypothesis. A rise and a plateau in both methods, with no decline up to 2000 genes, says that the panel of 500 is not too large for the pseudo-bulks. A decline that disappears after the bulk consistency filter points to platform-inconsistent genes, which only the real bulks can show. A decline in DeCovarT alone, present already on pseudo-bulks, points to the covariance estimate rather than to the genes.
